question: A 2.5-year-old boy has had fever for 7 days. Examination reveals bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue with cracked lips, cervical lymphadenopathy (2 cm), and erythema and oedema of both hands. Which additional feature, if present, would complete the classic diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Palpable purpura is the hallmark of HSP (IgA vasculitis), not Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki rash is a polymorphous exanthem — typically morbilliform or targetoid, not purpuric.

answers.text: Polymorphous skin rash (exanthem) involving the trunk and extremities

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The classic Kawasaki criteria are CREAM: Conjunctivitis (bilateral non-purulent), Rash (polymorphous exanthem), Erythema/oedema of hands/feet with later desquamation, Adenopathy (cervical >1.5 cm, usually unilateral), and Mouth changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips, injected pharynx). This child has all except the rash.

answers.text: Arthritis of the knee and ankle joints

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Arthritis can occur in Kawasaki disease but it is NOT one of the five classic diagnostic criteria. The CREAM mnemonic captures the five required features.
Kawasaki disease is not caused by streptococcus and ASO titre is not a diagnostic feature. An elevated ASO raises concern for acute rheumatic fever instead.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the CREAM mnemonic for Kawasaki disease. Classic diagnosis requires fever for ≥5 days plus at least 4 of 5 specific features. Distinguishing Kawasaki rash from HSP purpura is a common exam trap.
Correct. Remember CREAM: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Erythema/oedema of extremities, Adenopathy, Mouth changes. Fever ≥5 days plus 4 of these 5 features makes the classic diagnosis.
